objectives:
Course Objectives
1. Close reading skills
2. Key concepts and arguments in feminist and literary studies
3. Attention to politics of place in time
4. Ability to synthesize research and formulate questions
content:
Course Description
Inter-Asia cultural studies refers to a journal while also meaning an intellectual movement among and between peoples living in and moving across “Asia” – a geographic and political imaginary mediated through largely Anglophone imperial knowledge and semi-colonial, colonial, and post-colonial administrations in or toward competing forms of nation-statehood. In this course, we will focus on fiction and non-fiction in English (translations) and Chinese that address critical questions arising in local situations with trans-local resonance.

The first unit of readings begin with 19c and early 20c socialist anarchist and communist feminist discourse, that is, He Zhen, Engels, and Kollontai. Engels’s materialist historical narrative of the modern nuclear family, i.e. monogamous marriage and the state will accompany readings of Kollontai and He Zhen, each with early visions of liberation through abolishing inheritance based marriage-family form as cornerstone of private property and market society. The second unit moves to a USA post-(cold)war seventies and its radical women’s, gay and lesbian, and student liberation movements. We will read Shulamith Firestone, Gayle Rubin, Hortense Spillers and Kimberley Crenshaw, alongside Leslie Feinberg’s Stone Butch Blues, to revisit feminist revolutionary and radical critique at the crossroads of a post-cold war new (neoliberal) economic world order. In the third and final unit, we will read of one East Asian “miracle” state spawned in this new world order, the stakes and price for the peoples involved, especially women and/in families, in ever accelerating compressed aspirational re/productive labor – on the (market individualist) self and its others, at work and at home, with unintended effects for gender as class and sex as race (Hsu). In this final unit, we will read Kim Jiyoung Born 1984, and The Convenience Store World/Woman, with three of Cho Haejoang’s prescient analytic essays alongside Maria Mies on housewifization as ongoing production of disposable yet necessary labor and workers. Ursula Huws will help us think an ungendering (Spillers) of present day disposable workforce through ever expanding consumption  work.

For those interested in taking the class, please read the following in English or Chinese translation(s): 1) Friedrich Engels, The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State (1884; https://www.marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1884/origin-family/), 2) Leslie Feinberg, Stone Butch Blues (1993; https://www.lesliefeinberg.net/), 3) Cho Nam-Joo, Kim Jiyoung, born 1982 (2016), 4) Sayaka Murata, The Convenience Store World/Woman (2016).

Closely read and engage with the different texts. Select at least one novel and two to three critical essays toward a working paper engaging a topic that arises from the course in a final paper of eight to twelve pages (A4, font 12). Discuss the final paper topic with the instructor before writing. Evaluation: 1) bi-weekly reading responses (in-class writing) (30％), 2) individual or partnered presentations with outline (30％), and a final paper (40％).
